Nuclear Weapon Ban Treaty

| Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons | |
| --- | --- |
| Parties    Signatories | |
| Type | [Arms control](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_control "Arms control"), [nuclear disarmament](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament") |
| Signed | 20 September 2017[[1]](#cite_note-treatiesun-1) |
| Location | New York, U.S. |
| Sealed | 7 July 2017 |
| Effective | 22 January 2021[[2]](#cite_note-UN50-2) |
| Condition | 90 days after the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession has been deposited |
| Signatories | 95[[1]](#cite_note-treatiesun-1) |
| Parties | 75[[1]](#cite_note-treatiesun-1) ([complete list](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_parties_to_the_Treaty_on_the_Prohibition_of_Nuclear_Weapons "List of parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons")) |
| Depositary | [United Nations Secretary-General](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Secretary-General "United Nations Secretary-General") |
| Languages | [Arabic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"), [Chinese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"), [English](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), [French](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), [Russian](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language") and [Spanish](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") |
| Full text | |
| [Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Treaty%20on%20the%20Prohibition%20of%20Nuclear%20Weapons "wikisource:Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons") at [Wikisource](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikisource "Wikisource") | |

The **Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons** (**TPNW**), or the **Nuclear Weapon Ban Treaty**, is the first legally binding international agreement to comprehensively[*[dubious](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy_dispute#Disputed_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute") – [discuss](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Treaty_on_the_Prohibition_of_Nuclear_Weapons#not_comprehensive_since_prohibition_applies_only_for_parties "Talk:Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons")*] prohibit [nuclear weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon"), with the ultimate goal being their [total elimination](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament"). It was adopted on 7 July 2017, opened for signature on 20 September 2017, and entered into force on 22 January 2021.[[3]](#cite_note-guardian-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

For those states that are party to it, the treaty prohibits the development, [testing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_testing "Nuclear weapons testing"), production, stockpiling, [stationing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_sharing "Nuclear sharing"), [transfer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_proliferation "Nuclear proliferation"), use and threat of use of nuclear weapons, as well as assistance and encouragement to the prohibited activities. For nuclear-armed states joining the treaty, it provides for a time-bound framework for negotiations leading to the verified and irreversible elimination of its nuclear weapons programme.

A mandate adopted by the [United Nations General Assembly](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") on 23 December 2016 scheduled two sessions for negotiations: 27 to 31 March and 15 June to 7 July 2017.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The treaty passed on schedule on 7 July with 122 in favour, 1 against ([Netherlands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands")), and 1 official abstention ([Singapore](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore")). States that have joined the treaty are typically also members of [nuclear-weapon-free zones](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-weapon-free_zone "Nuclear-weapon-free zone"). None of the states that [possess nuclear weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_nuclear_weapons "List of states with nuclear weapons") have joined the treaty, nor have any of the states that participate in [nuclear sharing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_sharing "Nuclear sharing") or [extended nuclear deterrence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_umbrella "Nuclear umbrella") relationships, including [NATO members](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_states_of_NATO "Member states of NATO"), [Australia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Australia and weapons of mass destruction"), [Belarus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Belarus and weapons of mass destruction"), [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Japan and weapons of mass destruction"), and [South Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "South Korea and weapons of mass destruction").[[8]](#cite_note-UNTextAndVote-8)

According to its proponents, a treaty banning nuclear weapons will constitute an "unambiguous political commitment" to achieve and maintain a nuclear-weapon-free world.[[9]](#cite_note-9) However, unlike a comprehensive [nuclear weapons convention](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_convention "Nuclear weapons convention"), it was not intended to contain all of the legal and technical measures required to reach the point of elimination. Such provisions will instead be the subject of subsequent negotiations, allowing the initial agreement to be concluded relatively quickly and, if necessary, without the involvement of nuclear-armed states.[[10]](#cite_note-article36-10)

Proponents of the ban treaty believe that it will help stigmatize nuclear weapons, and serve as a catalyst for elimination.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Around two-thirds of the world's countries have pledged to work together "to fill the legal gap" in the existing international regime governing nuclear weapons,[[12]](#cite_note-12) and view a nuclear weapons–ban treaty as one option for achieving this objective.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

Nuclear weapons – unlike [chemical weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_weapons "Chemical weapons"), [biological weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_weapons "Biological weapons"), [anti-personnel landmines](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-personnel_landmines "Anti-personnel landmines") and [cluster munitions](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_munitions "Cluster munitions") – are not prohibited in a comprehensive and universal manner.[[14]](#cite_note-14) The [Non-Proliferation Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Proliferation_Treaty "Non-Proliferation Treaty") (NPT) of 1968 contains only partial prohibitions, and [nuclear-weapon-free zone](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-weapon-free_zone "Nuclear-weapon-free zone") treaties prohibit nuclear weapons only within certain geographical regions.

## Overview of provisions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Treaty_on_the_Prohibition_of_Nuclear_Weapons&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Overview of provisions")]

The *preamble* of the treaty[[15]](#cite_note-finalDraft-15) explains the motivation by the "catastrophic consequences" of a use of nuclear weapons, by the risk of their sheer existence, by the suffering of the *[hibakusha](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibakusha "Hibakusha")* (the surviving victims of the 1945 [atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki")) and the victims of nuclear tests, by "the slow pace of [nuclear disarmament](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament")" and by "the continued reliance on nuclear weapons in military and security concepts" like [deterrence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_deterrence "Nuclear deterrence"). It recognizes "the disproportionate impact of nuclear-weapon activities on indigenous peoples". It expresses compliance with existing law: the [UN charter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_charter "UN charter"), [international humanitarian law](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_humanitarian_law "International humanitarian law"), [international human rights law](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_human_rights_law "International human rights law"), the very first UN resolution adopted on 24 January 1946, the NPT, the [Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty") and its verification regime, as well as [nuclear-weapon-free zones](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-weapon-free_zone "Nuclear-weapon-free zone"). Furthermore, the "inalienable right" of peaceful use of [nuclear energy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") is emphasized. Finally, social factors for peace and disarmament are recognized: [participation of both women and men](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights"), education, public conscience, "international and regional organizations, non-governmental organizations, religious leaders, parliamentarians, academics and the *hibakusha*".

*Article 1* contains prohibitions against the development, testing, production, [stockpiling](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_reserve "Military reserve"), stationing, transfer, use and [threat](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threat "Threat") of use of nuclear weapons, as well as against assistance and encouragement to the prohibited activities. Finally, any direct or indirect "control over nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices" is forbidden.

*Article 2* requires each party to declare whether it had nuclear weapons of their own or deployed on its territory, including the elimination or conversion of related facilities.

*Article 3* requires parties that do not possess nuclear weapons to maintain their existing [IAEA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") safeguards and, if they have not already done so, to accept safeguards based on the model for non-nuclear-weapon states under the NPT.

*Article 4* sets out general procedures for negotiations with an individual nuclear-armed state becoming party to the treaty, including time limits and responsibilities. If that state has eliminated its nuclear weapons before becoming a party to the treaty, it mandates verification of that elimination by an unspecified "competent international authority", and the state must also conclude a safeguards agreement with the IAEA to provide credible assurance that it has not diverted nuclear material and has no undeclared nuclear material or activities. If that state has not yet destroyed its arsenal, it must negotiate with the "competent international authority" a time-bound plan for the verified and irreversible elimination of its nuclear weapons programme, which it will submit to the next meeting of signing states or to the next review conference, whichever comes first.

*Article 5* is about national implementation. *Article 6* requires environmental remediation and assistance for the victims of the use and testing of nuclear weapons. According to *Article 7*, states should assist each other to fulfil these purposes, with special responsibility of the nuclear powers. More generally, all state parties shall cooperate to facilitate the implementation of the treaty. *Article 8* fixes meetings of states parties, the costs of which are shared by the states according to the UN scale of assessment (*Article 9*). *Articles 10–12* are about the possibility of amendments, the settlement of disputes and the "goal of universal adherence of all States to the Treaty".

According to *Articles 13–15*, the treaty was open for signature from 20 September 2017 at the UN headquarters in New York. The "Treaty shall enter into force 90 days after the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession".

The **Xinjiang conflict** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 新疆冲突; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *xīnjiāng chōngtú*), also known as the **East Turkestan conflict**, **Uyghur–Chinese conflict** or **Sino–East Turkestan conflict** (as argued by the [East Turkistan Government-in-Exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Turkistan_Government-in-Exile "East Turkistan Government-in-Exile")),[[9]](#cite_note-9) is an ethnic geopolitical conflict in what is now [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")'s far-[northwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_China "Northwest China") [autonomous region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_regions_of_China "Autonomous regions of China") of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"), also known as East Turkestan. It is centred around the [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs"), a [Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") ethnic group who constitute a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority#Related_terms "Majority") (or 'relative majority'[[a]](#cite_note-11)) of the region's population.[[11]](#cite_note-12)[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDwyer20051–3-13)

In the 1930s, armed conflicts known as the Xinjiang Wars broke out during the [Warlord Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warlord_Era "Warlord Era") of the Republic of China and the Chinese Civil War, beginning with the [Kumul Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumul_Rebellion "Kumul Rebellion") which saw the establishment of the [First East Turkestan Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_East_Turkestan_Republic "First East Turkestan Republic") in 1933 as well as its destruction in 1934.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlimeš2015122-123-14) The [Second East Turkestan Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_East_Turkestan_Republic "Second East Turkestan Republic") was later founded in 1944 with the support of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") in the wake of the [Ili Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ili_Rebellion "Ili Rebellion"). Many of the Turkic peoples in Ili had close ties with the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union. As a result, many Turkic rebels fled to the Soviet Union and obtained Soviet assistance to create the Sinkiang Turkic People's Liberation Committee (STPNLC) in 1943 against Kuomintang rule during the Ili Rebellion.[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEForbes1986172–173-15) Since the [incorporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incorporation_of_Xinjiang_into_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Incorporation of Xinjiang into the People's Republic of China") of the region into the People's Republic of China, there h

The **Xinjiang internment camps**[[note 1]](#cite_note-10) are [internment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment "Internment") camps operated by the government of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") and the [Chinese Communist Party Provincial Standing Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party_Provincial_Standing_Committee "Chinese Communist Party Provincial Standing Committee"). [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") says that they have been used to indoctrinate [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") and other Muslims since 2017 as part of a "[Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_Against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism")", a policy announced in 2014 after the [May 2014 Ürümqi attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2014_%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi_attack "May 2014 Ürümqi attack").[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-fp-gulag-12) Xinjiang internment camps have been described as "the most extreme example of China's inhumane policies against Uighurs".[[9]](#cite_note-Kirby-2020-9) They were established as what are officially called **vocational education and training centers**[[note 2]](#cite_note-13) by the [government of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China").[[12]](#cite_note-14)[[13]](#cite_note-15) According to researcher [Adrian Zenz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Zenz "Adrian Zenz"), mass internments peaked in 2018 and have abated somewhat since then, with officials shifting focus towards forced labor programs.[[14]](#cite_note-16) Since then, the Chinese government has claimed the centers have been closed. Individuals in the camps have been shifted into the formal [penal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_system_in_China "Penal system in China"),[[15]](#cite_note-17) with remaining camps being converted into prisons or factories using forced labor.[[16]](#cite_note-18)[[17]](#cite_note-19)[[18]](#cite_note-20)

The camps were established in 2017 by [the administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping_Administration "Xi Jinping Administration") of CCP general secretary [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping").[[19]](#cite_note-Ramzy-2019-21)[[20]](#cite_note-22) Between 2017 and 2021 operations were led by [CCP Politburo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CCP_Politburo "CCP Politburo") member and [Xinjiang Party secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_Secretary_of_Xinjiang "Party Secretary of Xinjiang") [Chen Quanguo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Quanguo "Chen Quanguo").[[21]](#cite_note-23)[[22]](#cite_note-24) The camps are reportedly operated outside the [Chinese legal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_legal_system "Chinese legal system"); many Uyghurs have reportedly been interned without trial and no charges have been levied against them (held in [administrative detention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_detention "Administrative detention")).[[23]](#cite_note-arrests-skyrocketed-25)[[24]](#cite_note-26) Local authorities are reportedly holding hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs in these camps as well as members of other [ethnic minority groups in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_minority_groups_in_China "Ethnic minority groups in China"), for the [stated purpose of countering extremism and terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_Against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism") and promoting [social integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_integration "Social integration").[[25]](#cite_note-:80242-27)[[26]](#cite_note-28)[[27]](#cite_note-29)[[28]](#cite_note-Stroup-2019-30)[[29]](#cite_note-31)

In July 2019, UN ambassadors of 37 countries, predominantly in Africa and Asia, signed a joint letter to the [United Nations Human Rights Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council "United Nations Human Rights Council") defending China's policies in Xinjiang while 22 countries, mostly in North America and Europe, opposed them.[[30]](#cite_note-32)[[31]](#cite_note-33) In October 2020, 16 countries that defended China's policies in 2019 did not do so the following year.[[32]](#cite_note-axio_Mapp-34)

The internment of Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in the camps constituted the largest-scale [arbitrary detention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_detention "Arbitrary detention") of ethnic and religious minorities since [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[33]](#cite_note-Finley-2020-35)[[9]](#cite_note-Kirby-2020-9)[[34]](#cite_note-Rajagopalan-2020-36)[[35]](#cite_note-Niewenhuis-2020-37) In 2020, it was estimated that Chinese authorities may have detained up to 1.8 million[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*] people, mostly Uyghurs but also including [Kazakhs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhs_in_China "Kazakhs in China"), [Kyrgyz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrgyz_in_China "Kyrgyz in China") and other ethnic Turkic [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China "Islam in China"), [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_China "Christianity in China"), as well as some foreign citizens including [Kazakhstanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstanis "Kazakhstanis"), in these secretive internment camps located throughout the region.[[36]](#cite_note-38)[[2]](#cite_note-auto-2) In September 2020, the [Australian Strategic Policy Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Strategic_Policy_Institute "Australian Strategic Policy Institute") (ASPI) reported in its [Xinjiang Data Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_Data_Project "Xinjiang Data Project") that construction of camps continued despite government claims that their function was winding down.[[37]](#cite_note-Graham-Harrison-2020-39) There have been comparisons between the Xinjiang camps and the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution").[[38]](#cite_note-40)[[39]](#cite_note-41)[[40]](#cite_note-42)[[41]](#cite_note-43)

# Lens 2B.4 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler respect civilian protection, humanitarian law, prisoner treatment, necessity, and proportionality in military operations?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** — Xi did not respect civilian protection, humanitarian law, prisoner treatment, necessity, or proportionality across the active 2023 theaters: the **Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis** continued with PLA exercises around Taiwan without humanitarian-risk mitigation; the **South China Sea** grey-zone coercion against the Philippines intensified (10 November 2023 "control measures" at Second Thomas Shoal); the **Xinjiang** mass-internment / forced-labor apparatus continued under Xi's declared "success" framing (August 2023 visit); the **Hong Kong** NSL trials (47-pro-democracy politicians, Jimmy Lai) continued; the **Counterespionage Law** (effective July 2023) extended state authority over dual-use researchers and citizens; and **no IHL/LOAC compliance reform** was announced in 2023.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — civilian protection and humanitarian-law negatives

### 1. Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis continued without civilian-protection restraint

- **Claim A1.** Throughout 2023, the Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis (initiated August 2022) continued with PLA exercises, ADIZ incursions, naval patrols, and Coast Guard boardings. No IHL/LOAC compliance reform was announced; no humanitarian-notification mechanism for civilian-transit zones was established; no deconfliction protocol with Taiwanese civil aviation or maritime traffic was announced. The operational pressure around Taiwan was sustained without civilian-protection safeguards.
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis ("China initiated military maneuvers around Taiwan on 2 August 2022 … PLA exercises, maritime patrols and even Coast Guard boardings around the Taiwan Strait becoming routine in what has been defined as 'grey-zone tactics'").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian-protection restraint absent), 1B.5, 8G.6.

### 2. South China Sea grey-zone coercion against the Philippines continued without IHL restraint

- **Claim A2.** China's grey-zone coercion campaign against the Philippines continued through 2023, with the 10 November 2023 "control measures" against Philippine vessels at Second Thomas Shoal a representative incident. The campaign included water-cannoning and dangerous maneuvers against Philippine resupply missions, with documented risk to civilian crew. No 2023 IHL compliance reform was announced; no deconfliction framework was concluded.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 entry: "China imposes 'control measures' against Philippine vessels at a contested South China Sea location after a Philippine auxiliary ship entered the area which China deemed as infringing on its sovereignty").
  - **Source:** "South China Sea disputes" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes (records continued operational pattern).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian-protection restraint absent), 8G.5.

### 3. Xinjiang mass-internment apparatus continued under Xi's August 2023 "success" declaration

- **Claim A3.** Xi visited Xinjiang in August 2023 and publicly declared his policies there a "success." Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut was sentenced to life in prison in September 2023. The internment-camp and forced-labor apparatus — well-documented as the largest-scale arbitrary detention of an ethnic-religious minority since World War II (up to 1.8 million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims) — continued in modified form (camps converted to prisons and forced-labor factories) under Xi's declared success.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In August, President Xi visited Xinjiang ahead of the first anniversary of a damning United Nations report that detailed widespread abuses across Xinjiang—including targeting of cultural and religious practices, family separation, arbitrary arrests and detention, rapes, torture, and enforced disappearances—and concluded that Beijing's policies in the region 'may constitute crimes against humanity.' Xi pronounced that his policies in Xinjiang were a 'success' … In September, a court sentenced prominent Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut to life imprisonment").
  - **Source:** "Xinjiang internment camps" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps ("mass internments peaked in 2018 and have abated somewhat since then, with officials shifting focus towards forced labor programs").
  - **Source:** "Xinjiang conflict" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_conflict.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (strongly negative — civilian protection violated, no proportionality), 8D.5.

### 4. Hong Kong NSL trials continued with prolonged pre-trial detention

- **Claim A4.** In July 2023, the high-profile national-security trial of 47 pro-democracy politicians began. In October 2023, four former university student leaders were sentenced to two years in prison for "incitement to wound with intent" related to a 2021 student council resolution. In July 2023, Hong Kong police issued baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled activists abroad. Jimmy Lai's trial was scheduled for December 2023. The NSL prosecution rate at time of writing was ~100%. Many of these cases involved prolonged pre-trial detention and limited due-process access — neither necessity nor proportionality in civilian-protection terms.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In July, the high-profile national security trial of 47 pro-democracy politicians began. Another national security trial, of 75-year-old media tycoon Jimmy Lai, was slated to begin on December 18. In October, four former university student leaders were sentenced to two years in prison for 'incitement to wound with intent.' … In July, police issued baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled politicians and activists who reside abroad for offenses under the National Security Law. Police froze their bank accounts, interrogated their Hong Kong-based family members, and raided the homes of activists associated with them").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian-protection and due-process deficits), 8D.6.

### 5. Counterespionage Law (effective July 2023) expanded state authority over dual-use researchers and citizens

- **Claim A5.** The NPC Standing Committee passed a revised Counterespionage Law in April 2023, effective July 2023. It "restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data." After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security called on citizens to engage in counterespionage activity. This is a structural expansion of state authority over civilians, dual-use researchers, and journalists — not a civilian-protection measure.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("The revised Counterespionage Law gained the NPC standing committee's approval in April 2023 and took effect in July. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data. After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security called on ordinary citizens to engage in counterespionage activity").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian-rights expansion of state authority), 1B.9, 8F.1.

### 6. Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023) — religious-civilian-protection deterioration

- **Claim A6.** New Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues came into force in September 2023, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in CCP ideology, prohibiting "conflict between sects," and barring non-state-approved funding. Uyghur, Tibetan, Hui, and Christian religious practice — already heavily restricted — faced an additional structural instrument of state control. The May 2023 Najiaying Mosque protest in Yunnan (HRW-documented) showed the operational consequence.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("The Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues came into force in September. They impose further restrictions on religious activities, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in Chinese Communist Party ideology, and prohibiting them from 'creating conflicts … between sects' or receiving funding other than those approved by the state").
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian religious-freedom protection), 8D.4.

### 7. Patriotic Education Law (October 2023) — civilian-rights expansion

- **Claim A7.** The Patriotic Education Law signed by Xi on 24 October 2023 mandates patriotic education across all levels and types of schooling, requires museums and tourist sites to function as patriotic-education venues, requires internet platforms to produce "patriotic" content, and explicitly extends to Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and overseas Chinese. Article 33 mandates internet platforms to develop "new technologies and products to vividly carry out patriotic education." This is a structural expansion of state authority over civilian life.
  - **Source:** "Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic_Education_Law_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian-rights expansion), 8F.1, 2B.3.

### 8. Continued human-rights lawyers and journalists prosecuted in 2023

- **Claim A8.** Throughout 2023, human-rights lawyers (Xu Zhiyong 14 years, Ding Jiaxi 12 years, Guo Feixiong 8 years, Qin Yongpei 5 years, Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years, etc.) received long sentences; Wang Quanzhang, Wang Yu, and Bao Longjun were placed under house arrest; Yu Wensheng and his wife Xu Yan were arrested en route to a meeting with the EU ambassador in Beijing; journalist Yang Zewei was disappeared from Laos in May 2023 and reappeared in detention in Hunan; human-rights lawyer Lu Siwei was deported from Laos to China in September 2023. The pattern is a civilian-protection and due-process failure at scale.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china (multi-case documentation).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (negative — civilian-protection and due-process failures), 8D.7.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — partial restraint positives

### 9. No new kinetic war in 2023

- **Claim B1.** China did not initiate any new international armed conflict in 2023. The 10 November 2023 South China Sea confrontation did not escalate to direct armed clash; the LAC standoff with India did not produce 2023 kinetic engagements comparable to 2020 Galwan; the Taiwan operational pressure remained grey-zone rather than kinetic.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.4 (positive — no new kinetic war), 2B.2, 8G.

### 10. India LAC — bilateral architecture maintained
